learningObjectives: Waves transfer energy without transferring matter

questions.lo: Waves transfer energy without transferring matter
questions.q: What does a wave transfer as it travels across the surface of water?
options: Energy but not matter
Matter but not energy
Both the water and the energy together
Neither energy nor matter
questions.explain: A wave transfers energy from place to place without transferring matter. The water bobs up and down but is not carried along with the wave.

questions.lo: Waves transfer energy without transferring matter
questions.q: A ball floats on a pond. A wave passes underneath and travels on. What happens to the ball?
options: It is carried to the far side of the pond
It sinks to the bottom
It bobs up and down and stays roughly in place
It is pushed backwards then forwards to the edge
questions.explain: Because a wave carries energy, not matter, the ball just bobs up and down in place while the energy of the wave moves on.

questions.lo: Wave properties: amplitude, wavelength and frequency
questions.q: How is the wavelength of a transverse wave correctly measured?
options: From the rest line up to a crest
From a crest to the very next crest
From a crest to the nearest trough
From a trough back to the rest line
questions.explain: The wavelength is one complete cycle, so it is measured crest-to-crest (or trough-to-trough). Crest to the nearest trough is only half a wavelength.

questions.lo: Wave properties: amplitude, wavelength and frequency
questions.q: The frequency of a wave is measured in hertz (Hz). What does the frequency tell you?
options: How tall the wave is
How far the wave travels in total
How many complete waves pass a point each second
The speed of the wave in metres per second
questions.explain: Frequency is the number of complete waves passing a point each second, measured in hertz. It is not the same as amplitude (height) or speed.

questions.lo: Sound waves: longitudinal, need a medium, speed of sound
questions.q: Sound waves are described as longitudinal. What does this mean?
options: The particles vibrate at right angles to the wave's direction
The particles vibrate back and forth in the same direction the wave travels
The wave has no wavelength
The wave can only travel through a vacuum
questions.explain: In a longitudinal wave the particles vibrate back and forth along the same direction the wave travels, forming compressions and rarefactions.

questions.lo: Sound waves: longitudinal, need a medium, speed of sound
questions.q: Why can't you hear a sound made in space (a vacuum)?
options: Space is too cold to carry sound
There are no particles in a vacuum to pass the vibration on
Sound travels too fast in space to be heard
Light blocks the sound in space
questions.explain: Sound needs a medium (solid, liquid or gas). A vacuum has almost no particles, so there is nothing to pass the vibration on and the sound cannot travel.

questions.lo: Sound waves: longitudinal, need a medium, speed of sound
questions.q: In which of these does sound travel fastest?
options: Air
Water
A steel bar
A vacuum
questions.explain: Sound travels fastest when particles are closest together, so it is fastest in solids like steel and slowest in gases like air. It cannot travel in a vacuum at all.

questions.lo: Reflection and absorption of sound, echoes
questions.q: What is an echo?
options: Sound that has been absorbed by a soft surface
A sound wave that has reflected off a hard surface and returned
A sound with a very high pitch
Sound travelling through a vacuum
questions.explain: An echo is a reflection of sound. When a sound wave hits a hard surface it bounces back, and we hear the returning wave as an echo.

questions.lo: Reflection and absorption of sound, echoes
questions.q: An empty hall echoes, but once it is filled with curtains, carpets and soft seats the echo disappears. Why?
options: Soft materials reflect sound more strongly
Soft materials absorb the sound instead of reflecting it
Soft materials speed up the sound
Soft materials turn the sound into light
questions.explain: Soft materials such as carpet and curtains absorb sound rather than reflecting it, so there is little or no reflected sound to hear as an echo.

questions.lo: The human ear, hearing range and ultrasound
questions.q: What is the approximate hearing range of a healthy young human?
options: 2 Hz to 200 Hz
20 Hz to 20 000 Hz
200 Hz to 2000 Hz
questions.explain: The human auditory range is roughly 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz (20 kHz). Sound above this range is called ultrasound and cannot be heard by people.

questions.lo: The human ear, hearing range and ultrasound
questions.q: A dog whistle produces a sound at 25 000 Hz. Why can a dog hear it but a person cannot?
options: The whistle is too quiet for people
25 000 Hz is above the human hearing range but within a dog's
People have no ear drums
The sound is actually a light wave
questions.explain: 25 000 Hz is above the human hearing range of about 20 000 Hz, so it is ultrasound to us, but dogs can hear higher frequencies.

questions.lo: Amplitude and loudness, frequency and pitch
questions.q: You turn a speaker up so the same song is much louder. Which property of the sound waves has increased?
options: The frequency
The amplitude
The pitch
The wavelength
questions.explain: Loudness depends on amplitude, so a louder sound has a bigger amplitude. The pitch (frequency) is unchanged because it is still the same notes.

questions.lo: Amplitude and loudness, frequency and pitch
questions.q: A singer sings a much higher note but at the same volume. Which property of the sound has changed?
options: The amplitude has increased
The frequency has increased
The frequency has decreased
Nothing has changed
questions.explain: A higher-pitched note means a higher frequency. The volume (amplitude) is unchanged because it is the same loudness.

questions.lo: Light travels in straight lines and through a vacuum
questions.q: In a thunderstorm you see the lightning almost instantly but hear the thunder several seconds later. Why?
options: Sound is created after the light
Light travels much faster than sound
Sound travels in curves and light in straight lines
Your ears react more slowly than your eyes
questions.explain: Light travels far faster (about 300 000 000 m/s) than sound (about 340 m/s in air), so the light reaches you almost instantly while the sound arrives later.

questions.lo: Reflection of light and the law of reflection
questions.q: A ray of light hits a flat mirror at an angle of incidence of 40 degrees, measured from the normal. What is the angle of reflection?
options: 50 degrees
40 degrees
80 degrees
0 degrees
questions.explain: By the law of reflection, the angle of reflection always equals the angle of incidence, so it is also 40 degrees. Both are measured from the normal.

questions.lo: Refraction of light
questions.q: A straw in a glass of water looks bent at the surface. What causes this?
options: Reflection of light off the water
Refraction as light changes speed and bends at the water surface
The straw actually bending in the water
Absorption of light by the water
questions.explain: This is refraction: as light passes from the water into the air it changes speed and bends (changes direction), so the straw appears bent to your eye.

questions.lo: Colour and the visible spectrum
questions.q: When a prism splits white light, which order do the colours of the visible spectrum appear in?
options: Violet, blue, green, yellow, orange, red
Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet
Green, blue, red, yellow, violet, orange
Red, yellow, blue only
questions.explain: White light splits into the visible spectrum in the order red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet. Red bends the least and violet the most.

questions.lo: Colour and the visible spectrum
questions.q: Why does a red apple look red in white light?
options: It absorbs red light and reflects the others
It reflects red light and absorbs the other colours
It gives out its own red light
It refracts red light into your eyes
questions.explain: A red object reflects red light to your eyes and absorbs the other colours of the spectrum, so it appears red.

questions.lo: The eye and camera
questions.q: In both the eye and a camera, what does the convex lens do?
options: It produces its own light
It refracts light to focus a sharp image on the retina or sensor
It absorbs all the light so none passes through
It reflects the light back out
questions.explain: A convex lens refracts (bends) light to focus a clear image on the light-sensitive retina in the eye, or on the sensor or film in a camera.

questions.lo: Opaque, translucent and transparent materials
questions.q: Why does an opaque object such as a book cast a sharp shadow?
options: It lets all light pass straight through it
It blocks the light, which travels in straight lines and cannot bend around it
It absorbs sound as well as light
It reflects all the light back to the source
questions.explain: An opaque object blocks light. Because light travels in straight lines it cannot bend around the object to fill the gap behind it, so a shadow forms.

specSource: National Curriculum in England: science programme of study, Key Stage 3; Physics — Waves
